title.en: Exception Groups and except*: Many Errors at Once

description.en: Python 3.11 can raise several unrelated errors as one ExceptionGroup and handle each kind with except*. Learn why a plain except cannot see inside a group and how leftovers are re-raised.

story_variants.en:
## Many Things Can Go Wrong At Once

"So far, an exception has been a single thing," Vaathiyaar says. "One `raise`, one `except`. But what if you run five jobs side by side and three of them fail for different reasons? Throwing only the first error hides the other two."

Python 3.11 added **exception groups** for exactly this. An `ExceptionGroup` is an exception that *contains a list of other exceptions*.

### Raising a group

```
errors = [ValueError("bad row 3"), KeyError("id"), ValueError("bad row 6")]
raise ExceptionGroup("import failed", errors)
```

The first argument is a message and the second is a **non-empty** list of exceptions. Python refuses an empty list.

### Catching with `except*`

A normal `except ValueError` does **not** catch a group, even when the group holds a `ValueError`. The group is a different type. You need `except*`:

```
try:
    run_everything()
except* ValueError as eg:
    print(len(eg.exceptions), "value errors")
except* KeyError as eg:
    print(len(eg.exceptions), "key errors")
```

Each `except*` clause takes **its own slice** of the group, and `eg` is a smaller group holding only the matching errors. Every clause that has something to catch runs, not only the first. Anything left unmatched is re-raised afterwards as a group.

> **Vaathiyaar's note:** `asyncio.TaskGroup` (also new in 3.11) raises an `ExceptionGroup` when several tasks fail. `except*` is how you handle it.

Today you build `run_batch`, which keeps going after a failure and reports every error together. Then you flatten a nested group.

explanation.en: Collect each failure instead of stopping at the first
Bundle every error into one exception
Take the ValueError members as a smaller group
The next clause takes its own slice of what is left

instruction.en: Implement `run_batch(funcs)`. Call each function in order without stopping at failures. If all succeed, return the list of results. If any raised, raise `ExceptionGroup("batch failed", errors)` with every error, in call order, after the last function has run. The code below the function then prints how many `ValueError` and `KeyError` members the group held (expected: `ValueError: 2` then `KeyError: 1`).

en: Keep two lists, `results` and `errors`, and wrap each call in try/except Exception.
Do the raise after the loop, only if `errors` is not empty.
`raise ExceptionGroup("batch failed", errors)`; return `results` otherwise.

instruction.en: Implement `flatten(group)`: return the exception type names (`type(e).__name__`) at the leaves of a possibly nested exception group, in order. A member that is itself a group must be searched, not listed. Then print `flatten(nested)` (expected: `['ValueError', 'KeyError', 'TypeError']`).

practice_challenges.starter_code:
def flatten(group):
    """Return the names of the exception types at the leaves of a (possibly nested) group, in order."""
    pass

nested = ExceptionGroup("outer", [
    ValueError("a"),
    ExceptionGroup("inner", [KeyError("b"), TypeError("c")]),
])
print(flatten(nested))

en: `group.exceptions` is a tuple of members; loop over it.
Test a member with `isinstance(e, BaseExceptionGroup)`.
For a nested group, recurse and `extend` your list with the result.

practice_challenges.test_code:
g = ExceptionGroup("g", [OSError("x"), ExceptionGroup("h", [ExceptionGroup("i", [ValueError("y")]), KeyError("z")]), TypeError("w")])
assert flatten(g) == ["OSError", "ValueError", "KeyError", "TypeError"], "recurse into nested groups and keep the order"
assert flatten(ExceptionGroup("one", [ValueError("v")])) == ["ValueError"]

under_the_hood.summary: An ExceptionGroup bundles several exceptions into one; except* splits the group by type, runs each matching clause on its slice, and re-raises whatever nothing handled.

steps.title: Why one exception is not enough
steps.body: A normal `raise` unwinds the stack with exactly one exception object. When several independent jobs fail (concurrent tasks, a batch import, a set of validators) the first error wins and the rest are lost. An `ExceptionGroup` keeps all of them in a single object that can still travel up the stack.

left.label: One exception
left.code:
raise ValueError("bad row 3")
# the other failures never surface

right.label: An exception group
right.code:
raise ExceptionGroup("import failed", [
    ValueError("bad row 3"),
    KeyError("id"),
])

steps.title: A group is an exception holding exceptions
steps.body: `ExceptionGroup(message, excs)` stores the message in `.message` and the members in `.exceptions`, a tuple. The list must be non-empty, so an empty one raises `ValueError`. Members may themselves be groups, so a group can be a tree. Members of `ExceptionGroup` must be `Exception` subclasses; for things like `KeyboardInterrupt` Python uses `BaseExceptionGroup`.

steps.title: Plain except does not match a group
steps.body: `except ValueError` asks whether the raised object *is a* `ValueError`. A group is an `ExceptionGroup`, not a `ValueError`, so the clause does not match even if a `ValueError` is inside. `except*` instead asks which *members* match, and handles them.

stepDescriptions.description: The group is not a ValueError, so a plain clause does not match. (In real code you cannot mix except and except* in one try; this shows the contrast.)
except* looks inside the group for ValueError members.
eg is a new group with just the matching members; its .exceptions holds ValueError(1).

steps.title: Each except* takes its slice
steps.body: Python walks the except* clauses in order. Each one splits off the members it matches, runs its block with them, and passes the remainder to the next clause. Unlike plain `except`, more than one clause can run for one raise. Whatever nothing matched is raised again, as a group, when the `try` finishes.

steps.title: Splitting by hand and the rules
steps.body: `group.split(ValueError)` returns `(matching, rest)` and `group.subgroup(ValueError)` returns only the matching part. Both keep the nesting shape and the message. Inside `except*` you cannot use `return`, `break` or `continue`, and a bare `except*` is not allowed; you must name the types. A single plain exception caught by `except*` arrives wrapped in a group with an empty message.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Use ExceptionGroup when several things can fail independently, and except* to handle each kind. A plain except will not see inside a group, and leftovers are re-raised, never lost.
